title: Gender-specific labor shocks reallocate household consumption without changing total child-product spending
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35118, Gender-Specific Economic Shocks and Household Bargaining Power
geography: United States; heterosexual households, product-level consumption patterns, and US industrial robot and fracking shocks

observations.period: 2026 paper; machine-learning index built from product-level consumption patterns

denominator.unit: single-men and single-women consumption data; abstract does not disclose the analytic sample count

gendered_goods_index.value: The paper develops an index quantifying the gendered nature of consumer goods from single-men and single-women consumption patterns

household_application.value: The index is used to study how gender-specific labor-market shocks influence spending within heterosexual households

bargaining_link.value: Consumption allocation is treated as an outcome through which relative economic position may appear inside households

observations.method: Machine-learning classification using product-level consumption patterns of single men and single women, combined with analysis of household spending responses to gender-specific labor-market shocks.
observations.uncertainty: The index measures product-purchase associations rather than preferences or bargaining directly; the abstract does not disclose the full data construction, sample counts, confidence intervals, or all household controls.
observations.subgroup: Single men, single women, and heterosexual households with different relative labor-market exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Product differences can reflect income, age, household composition, location, or marketing rather than gendered bargaining power; spending allocation is not the same as welfare or decision authority.

observations.period: US industrial robot adoption shock; household consumption response

denominator.unit: heterosexual households exposed to local industrial robot adoption; abstract does not disclose the analytic count

relative_shock.value: Industrial robot adoption worsened men's relative economic position

consumption_reallocation.value: Household consumption shifted toward products predominantly purchased by single women

total_children_products.value: Robot exposure did not significantly alter total spending on children's products

daughter_son_mix.value: Robot exposure reallocated spending toward products more commonly purchased for daughters than for sons

observations.method: Household consumption analysis linked to local industrial robot exposure, using the gendered-goods index to distinguish product composition from total spending.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract does not provide effect sizes, exposure units, identification details, or the full child-product classification; the result does not establish changes in child wellbeing, parental time, or household decision rights.
observations.subgroup: Households facing industrial robot exposure that worsens men's relative economic position; child-product effects are separated by daughter/son association.
observations.counterinterpretation: Robot exposure can change local prices, employment, income, household composition, or product availability; the consumption shift may not be caused by bargaining power alone.

observations.period: US fracking expansion shock; household consumption response

denominator.unit: heterosexual households exposed to fracking-driven demand for young and less-skilled men; abstract does not disclose the analytic count

relative_shock.value: Fracking expanded demand for young and less-skilled men

men_favored_goods.value: Evidence of increased spending on goods favored by single men was suggestive but less robust

cross_shock_boundary.value: Robot and fracking shocks do not produce symmetric or equally robust consumption responses

observations.method: Comparative household-consumption analysis using fracking exposure as a positive labor-demand shock for a male-skewed workforce and the gendered-goods index.
observations.uncertainty: The abstract labels this evidence suggestive and less robust; it does not establish a precise causal effect, bargaining mechanism, or durable household welfare change.
observations.subgroup: Households in places exposed to fracking expansion, particularly those with young and less-skilled male labor-market exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Fracking can alter housing costs, migration, local prices, work schedules, and household composition, any of which may affect consumption independently of bargaining power.
